idiom_name: deinit + ARC deallocation (with defer / withExtendedLifetime for scope control)
implementation_notes: Swift's release point is the class deinitializer: deinit is called automatically just before an instance is deallocated, which ARC triggers as soon as the last strong reference goes away, so no explicit Dispose call is required and superclass deinitializers are chained for you. Because release follows the last reference rather than a lexical scope, the scope-deterministic spellings are defer { resource.close() } (runs on every exit path including thrown errors) and keeping the instance referenced only where it should live (withExtendedLifetime keeps it alive deliberately). deinit takes no parameters, cannot throw and cannot be called directly, so a release that must report an error needs a separate throwing close()/shutdown() that callers invoke explicitly; unowned/weak references are never released by the borrower, which encodes the borrowed-resource exclusion in the ownership model.
pitfalls: A retain cycle (closure capturing self, a strong delegate) keeps the last reference alive, so deinit never runs and the resource is never released - deinit is not a leak net.
deinit must not throw or assume the instance is still fully connectable; error-reporting cleanup belongs in an explicit close().

Release timing follows the last reference, so a resource captured by an escaping closure or a global cache lives longer than the creating scope; use defer or an explicit close when the lifetime must be lexical.
